title: Bruschetta al Pomodoro
author: Marco Bellini
desc: Bruschetta al Pomodoro is the simplest of Italian appetizers — grilled bread rubbed with garlic and piled high with juicy, ripe tomatoes, basil, and good olive oil.
longDesc: Bruschetta long predates the tomato topping most associate with it today — the word itself refers to the technique of grilling bread over coals (from the Roman dialect bruscare, 'to roast'). The tomato-basil version became the definitive style only after tomatoes arrived in Italy from the Americas.
ingredients: 1 loaf rustic Italian bread (such as Pane Toscano or ciabatta), sliced 2cm thick
2 garlic cloves, 1 minced and 1 left whole
15 fresh basil leaves, torn, plus more for garnish
60 ml (¼ cup) extra virgin olive oil, plus more for brushing
Salt and freshly ground black pepper, to taste
steps: In a bowl, combine the diced tomatoes, minced garlic, torn basil, olive oil, and red wine vinegar. Season with salt and pepper and let sit for 10–15 minutes to let the flavors meld.
Brush the bread slices lightly with olive oil on both sides.
Grill or toast the bread until golden and lightly charred at the edges, about 1–2 minutes per side.
While still warm, rub each slice once with the whole peeled garlic clove — it grates against the rough toasted surface for a subtle, fragrant hit.
Spoon the tomato mixture generously over each slice just before serving, letting some juices soak into the bread.
Garnish with extra basil and a final drizzle of olive oil. Serve immediately.
chefTips: Only assemble bruschetta right before serving — the bread turns soggy if topped too early.
Use the ripest, most flavorful tomatoes you can find; this dish has nowhere to hide mediocre ingredients.
Draining excess tomato juice for a minute in a sieve keeps the topping from making the bread soggy too fast.
commonMistakes: Topping the bread too far in advance, leading to a soggy base.
Skipping the garlic rub on the toasted bread, which is a key layer of flavor.
storage: Best eaten immediately. The tomato topping can be refrigerated separately for up to 1 day; toast bread fresh.
reheating: Not recommended — bruschetta is meant to be eaten fresh and crisp.
healthBenefits: Rich in lycopene from tomatoes, an antioxidant linked to heart health.
Uses heart-healthy olive oil as the primary fat.
culturalNote: In Italy, bruschetta is typically eaten as a starter or snack, never as a main course — a distinctly Italian-American adaptation turned it into more of an entrée-style dish abroad.
